title: Leonard Feather's Encyclopedia of Jazz and the need for first-hand tape
summary: Johnston explains why she wants Gil's own account on tape rather than printed sources such as Feather's encyclopedia.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: I'd love to hear you talk a little bit about that because even though I've had some training in music, I'm not a composer or a professional musician. I've a PhD in literature and I'm a theater historian, but my work crosses the lines. But anyway, although I read music, I certainly don't place myself in your category or anywhere near it. (LAUGHTER).

But what I'm simply saying is that last night I was looking at Leonard Feather's book which I don't think very much of in many ways, but I was looking at his notations and the bars in which he was showing, in the passages in which he was showing how a jazz musician could understand the horizontal line, whereas the classical musician would have difficulty because he is used to looking at the vertical line.
And I realise that if I had to start now, that I don't think I'd be able to deal with what I was looking at last night.
I know, but I didn't know it had any actual music in it.
Oh yes, yes, yes. It does.
..........something that Leonard wrote. It says when you were born and all that..........
I have a lot of that, but you see we need it on tape and I'd much rather have it come from you than simply to read into it what somebody else has written.
